How is Artificial Intelligence (AI) Used by Lawyers?

The news and the internet as well as legal publications are rife with stories of lawyers citing false or fake legal citations in legal briefs in courts worldwide. AI is known to hallucinate or make things up as if trying to please the user. Legal briefs cite legal precedence (previously decided cases) to support legal arguments the attorney is trying to make on behalf of a client. When a lawyer asks AI to find a case supporting a particular legal theory, in a particular jurisdiction, AI will predict the statistically most likely next word rather than searching for verified facts in a database creating what is known as hallucinations.

Lawyers need be cautious because submitting a client's personal facts into a general AI database which makes confidential information public violates the client's attorney-client privilege.

Lawyers can use AI to assist and streamline brief writing but must verify every legal citation as well as the descriptions or applications AI may give in applying those cases to the facts and the law. AI does not eliminate the need for an attorney, but it can assist, and, in some cases, expedite the attorney's work product. AI work is to be treated by a lawyer as if the work was done by a law student or first year associate attorney.

While not all courts require it, lawyers are advised to acknowledge in their work if being submitted to a court, where and to what extent they used AI. Lawyers must also comply with the American Bar Association (ABA) rules of professional conduct regarding competence, client communication, reasonable fees, confidentiality, candor toward the tribunal and the unauthorized practice of law as well as local state rules of professional conduct.

Lawyers must also be mindful not only of their own work but if a colleague submits false case citations or applications of case law, the attorney must advise the court of same. In a case reported by the New York Times in June 2026, a Federal Judge in Mississippi sanctioned lawyers on both sides after they both used AI to cite fake legal cases and neither pointed to the other's submission of fake caselaw.

Lawyers should also add information that they are using AI in their retainers, so clients are on notice.

In my family law practice, we use a closed, encrypted AI program developed for lawyers, so no information is used to train AI models or is distributed publicly. We attempted to use AI to write a factual history of our client's case to date. The AI did not follow our instructions, ignored facts that were submitted by us, and missed the points we were trying to make. In another case, we tried to use AI to assist in preparing a summation after trial. AI could not properly cite from the transcripts (and in certain instances, completely made up the citations).

In a recent Wall Street Journal article, People Are Using AI for Divorce Advice and It's Driving Their Lawyers Crazy, November 2, 2026, family law attorneys complained about the list of questions sent by their clients, longer than the document the lawyer was working on, generated by AI. Our office, as well, has received long lists of questions which to answer properly would take hours of time, time that would need to be billed to the client, for information not necessarily related to their case or helpful to them.

In our family law practice, two clients sent us long lists of questions which we immediately identified as AI-generated and which the clients readily admitted. In the one case, we'd asked the wife to review a list of discovery we were prepared to seek from the husband. The wife responded with an AI-generated request for documents well beyond the issues at hand. If we had simply passed that on to opposing counsel, there would be objections and even if produced, more documents than relevant or necessary, resulting in greater fees incurred by our client. In the other case, our client, the mother, is seeking custody of her two minor children. Her questions were about child custody, but the questions had nothing to do with the practical realities of her case and answering them would have taken considerable time.

In both cases, answering the AI generated questions would have cost the clients additional unnecessary fees and not helped their understanding of their cases. In both instances a meeting with each client in which their concerns were heard and answered in real time was the more expeditious and less costly manner of proceeding.

As family law attorneys we are used to clients seeking legal advice from their friends, family, the manicurist at the nail salon, group chats on Facebook, divorce support groups and online sites.

We are aware of people who advertise themselves as coaches and experts regarding areas of family law online for which these "experts" charge for their services. Using the word "narcissist" as a search term will bring up ex judges, attorneys, therapists all availing their services to litigants in family law cases, presumptively with a narcissist, at a cost to the litigant. To the litigants out there, AI-generated questions are not necessarily smarter or better than the questions you can ask yourself. If your lawyer can't answer your questions or you have lost confidence in your attorney to answer your questions, you should speak with the attorney and if still uncomfortable or lacking confidence, choose another attorney.

We are also used to litigants who represent themselves because they can't afford an attorney or because they believe they are their best advocate and certainly as to facts, the litigant who self represents has an edge up on the attorney who learns the facts from their client. The attorney, however, knows how to present facts, even bad facts, in a manner that can help their client.

Family law cases are fact specific. Different jurisdictions and different judges view things differently. Each state has its own laws re divorce and family law. While some aspects of family law are nationwide such as "best interest of the child" as to child custody, what best interest consists of may vary state by state and judge by judge. Some jurisdictions have adopted legal presumptions of joint custody, others have not. Because of the fact-intensive underpinnings of family law cases and the knowledge of experienced practitioners as to how to frame an argument with accurate citations and factual knowledge before judges in their jurisdiction, an attorney working for you is better than AI.

Because family law cases are so fact specific is why client use of AI is troublesome and can be costly. Clients ask AI questions without having an "understanding" of the full factual history and the procedural posture of the case. AI spews out 50 irrelevant questions that the attorney is asked to answer.

AI is a tool. Like the advent of legal research being conducted online in the 1990's, replacing legal research done with law books that are now only props in a TV show or a lawyer's office, AI too is a tool we are only just beginning to learn how to use to our best advantage. Hopefully it will assist attorneys and help reduce billable hours especially as to discovery review (production and review of documents). However, it cannot replace an attorney, at least not yet.

This article was originally published on Forbes.com
